title: 32. Enhancing team-based learning in animal science through Lego Serious Play®: A culturally responsive approach in the Cal Poly Bull Test Program.
content:
Abstract
Effective teamwork and relational trust are essential in committee-driven, student led agricultural programs where collaborative decision-making directly influences program outcomes. The Cal Poly Bull Test Program operates through two primary committees, Bull Management and Sale Management, each responsible for distinct but interdependent functions that benefit from strong interpersonal insight and shared understanding. To strengthen relational awareness and enhance collaborative functioning, we piloted Lego Serious Play® (LSP®) as an innovative, experiential teaching strategy during a 90-minute seminar session with committee members (n = 13). LSP® is grounded in constructivist and constructionist learning theory and uses structured model building and reflective dialogue to uncover individual perspectives and foster group meaning-making. Participants first constructed individual models representing the strengths, skills, experiences, and beliefs they bring to their respective subcommittee, then shared the meaning of their models in facilitated narrative reflection. In the second phase, committee members collaboratively built a single integrated model incorporating elements from each individual build to represent what they collectively bring to the broader Bull Test Program, requiring negotiation of meaning, mutual recognition, and intentional inclusion of diverse contributions. Immediately following the activity, participants completed brief likert rating scales assessing perceived general learning and dimensions of culturally responsive teaching for adult learners. On a five-point scale, participants reported positive perceptions across culturally responsive teaching domains, including General Learning (M = 3.84, SD = 0.71), Respect and Connectedness (M = 3.88, SD = 0.73), Choice and Personal Relevance (M = 3.95, SD = 0.68), Challenge and Engagement (M = 3.97, SD = 0.58), and Authenticity and Effectiveness (M = 4.05, SD = 0.62). These descriptive results suggest that participants perceived the LSP® activity as engaging and supportive of culturally responsive learning experiences in which their identities, perspectives, and agency were intentionally integrated into committee work. In animal science programs, students often collaborate in high-responsibility, team-based environments where livestock management, data interpretation, and sales coordination require trust and clear communication. These interactive lessons provide more broad engagement across animal science curricula to support group-based activities in the classroom, and not limited to livestock management experiences. Approaches that surface individual strengths and lived experiences may strengthen the relational foundations necessary for effective collaboration in these applied settings. The activity’s emphasis on respect, narrative sharing, learner choice, and co-construction aligns with culturally responsive pedagogy by positioning students as contributors of valuable knowledge rather than passive recipients of technical content. By externalizing tacit knowledge through metaphor and integrating individual contributions into a shared model, LSP® may enhance teamwork, shared purpose, and collaborative decision making. Although limited by a small sample size and self-reported data, these findings support further exploration of experiential pedagogies within animal science education.
